title: Third Day Morning: Creator and Keeper

sections.heading: Remembering who you are
sections.text: Most High God, everything that exists belongs to you. You made the whole creation by your word, you hold it together by your power, and nothing is outside your rule. And still, you are not distant from us. You are the Father who shows mercy, the God who gives grace, the one who comforts your people, and the protector of those you have saved.
theological_themes: God is Creator, Sustainer, and ruler over all things.
God’s sovereign majesty is held together with his fatherly mercy and comfort toward his people.

scripture_references.connection: This passage teaches that all things were created through and for Christ and that all things hold together in him, grounding the prayer’s confession that creation belongs to God and is sustained by his power.
Paul names God as the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, which directly supports the prayer’s confidence that the sovereign Creator is also tender toward his people.

sections.heading: Thanking you for the gifts you have given us
sections.text: You have not forgotten us. You have come near, kept us, and given us a rich inheritance: your Holy Scriptures, the good news that brings joy, and Jesus Christ, the Savior of our souls. These are gifts we could never have earned and must never take lightly.
theological_themes: God’s people receive spiritual riches as an inheritance from his mercy.
Scripture, the gospel, and Christ himself are gifts of grace and means of salvation.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes the Scriptures as able to make a person wise for salvation through faith in Christ and as sufficient for equipping God’s people, supporting the prayer’s gratitude for Scripture as a precious inheritance.
Peter speaks of God’s mercy giving believers a living hope and an imperishable inheritance kept for them, which fits the prayer’s thanksgiving for God’s preserving care and gospel gifts.

sections.heading: Coming to you only through Jesus
sections.text: We come to you in the name of Jesus. We do not bring our record, our goodness, or our promises as the reason you should receive us. We cling to his righteousness alone. We ask you to look on his obedience, his suffering, and his death for sinners—the way he fully honored your law and bore its penalty for us. By his blood, declare us righteous. By his risen life, save us completely. By your Spirit, unite us to him and keep us in him.
theological_themes: Believers approach God through Christ alone, not through their own righteousness.
Christ’s obedience and suffering fulfill the law and provide the basis for justification.
Salvation includes justification by Christ’s blood, life through his resurrection, and union with him by the Spirit.

scripture_references.connection: Paul rejects any righteousness of his own and seeks the righteousness from God that comes through faith in Christ, matching the prayer’s appeal to Christ’s righteousness alone.

Paul links justification with Christ’s blood and salvation with Christ’s life, giving strong biblical grounding for the prayer’s request to be justified by his death and saved by his living intercession.

This passage explains that God dealt with sin through his Son so that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled, supporting the prayer’s language about Christ honoring the law in both obedience and judgment.

sections.heading: Learning to follow him whatever you choose for us
sections.text: Teach us to take up the cross and follow Jesus. Let your grace make us ready for whatever you wisely appoint. Make us willing for you to choose our portion—what we keep and what we lose, what we suffer and what we enjoy. We do not trust our own wisdom enough to demand our own way. We want to receive our lives from your hand.
theological_themes: Discipleship means self-denial and following Christ in costly obedience.
God’s providence is wiser than human preference, and grace makes his people willing to receive his will.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus defines discipleship as denying oneself, taking up the cross daily, and following him, which directly grounds the prayer’s desire to follow Christ in costly obedience.
James warns against presumptuous control over the future and teaches believers to say, ‘if the Lord wills,’ supporting the prayer’s surrender of future gain, loss, suffering, and enjoyment to God.

sections.heading: Using prosperity rightly and enduring hardship faithfully
sections.text: If you give us prosperity, keep us from being trapped by it. Help us use your gifts with open hands, not waste them, worship them, or turn them into excuses for sin. And when hardship is necessary for our good, help us receive it with patience and even with a steady joy, trusting that you are not careless with our pain.
theological_themes: Material blessing is good but spiritually dangerous when it becomes an idol or is misused.
Affliction can be used by God for the good and holiness of his people, though it remains painful.

scripture_references.connection: Paul instructs the rich not to set their hope on wealth but on God, and to use their resources for good, supporting the prayer’s request to use prosperity without being ensnared by it.

Hebrews teaches that God’s discipline is painful but intended for holiness and the peaceful fruit of righteousness, giving biblical shape to the prayer’s request for patient submission under necessary affliction.

sections.heading: Keeping us from sin and bringing us home
sections.text: When we are tempted to wander from you, block the path that would lead us away. Wake up in us a real hatred of sin. Loosen our grip on this present evil age, and train our hearts to want you more than what cannot last. Keep assuring us that, in the end, you will bring us into Immanuel’s land, where your people are home with you, sickness is gone, sorrow is over, and your light never fails.
theological_themes: God’s preserving grace restrains his people from wandering and deepens hatred of sin.
Christians are being weaned from the present evil age and taught to long for the final home with God.
The hope of the new creation includes the end of sickness, sorrow, darkness, and death.

scripture_references.connection: Paul says Christ gave himself to deliver us from the present evil age according to the Father’s will, supporting the prayer’s desire to be freed from worldly attachment.
Jude praises God as the one able to keep believers from stumbling and present them blameless with joy, grounding the prayer’s request for God to guard us when we are tempted to wander.
John’s vision of God dwelling with his people and wiping away every tear supports the prayer’s hope for the final home where sickness, sorrow, and death are gone.
This verse describes the coming world where God’s servants need no sun because the Lord gives them light, illuminating the prayer’s image of a land where the light never fails.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original phrase 'thy dispensations' is used in an older providential sense, meaning God’s ordered dealings or appointed circumstances, not modern dispensational theology.

The line about afflictions being 'necessary' can be pastorally sensitive. The adaptation preserves the idea that God can use hardship for holiness while avoiding any implication that sufferers can easily identify or explain the exact necessity of each pain.
The phrase 'Immanuel’s land' was rendered as the final home of God’s people in the presence of Christ, drawing on new creation imagery rather than specifying a detailed intermediate-state theology.
significant_interpretive_choices: 'Made mention of his righteousness only' was interpreted as an appeal to Christ’s righteousness as the sole ground of acceptance before God, not as a general admiration of Jesus’ moral example.

'Magnified the law both in its precepts and penalty' was rendered as Christ fully honoring God’s law by his obedience and by bearing its penalty for sinners, preserving the original’s Reformed atonement logic.
'Hedge up our way' was paraphrased as God blocking paths that would lead us away, keeping the concrete image of restraining providence without directly reproducing the older wording.
